name: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) for Discrete Combinatorial Actions
key_paper: Schulman, J., Wolski, F., Dhariwal, P., Radford, A., & Klimov, O. (2017). Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms. arXiv:1707.06347. OpenAI technical report.
algorithm_description: PPO is an on-policy policy gradient algorithm that improves training stability by clipping the surrogate objective, preventing excessively large policy updates. At each iteration, it collects a batch of trajectories under the current policy, then optimizes a clipped importance-weighted objective (PPO-Clip) or a KL-penalized objective (PPO-KL) using multiple mini-batch gradient steps. The clipping ratio epsilon (typically 0.1-0.2) constrains how far the new policy can deviate from the old one per update, acting as a trust region without the expensive second-order computation of TRPO. PPO alternates between data collection and multiple epochs of gradient updates on the collected batch, making it relatively sample-efficient among on-policy methods. A value-function critic is trained in parallel to estimate the advantage function, reducing variance in the policy gradient estimate.
action_space_handling: Standard PPO treats each action dimension independently with a factored (independent) policy head — each element of the multi-hot output vector gets a separate Bernoulli or categorical distribution. For combinatorial set actions (choose k from N), PPO can be adapted via: (1) a flat multi-hot head where N independent Bernoulli logits are output and sampled independently, post-filtered to enforce k; (2) an autoregressive factored policy where each number is sampled one at a time conditioned on previous selections; or (3) a Gumbel-top-k reparameterization to directly sample exactly k items. The standard PPO formulation does not natively handle combinatorial constraints — these require explicit adaptation.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: The most common PPO adaptation for k-of-N selection is a two-stage approach: (1) the policy network outputs N logits over the ball pool; (2) either top-k selection (argmax-based, non-differentiable) or stochastic sampling without replacement (Gumbel-top-k, differentiable) is applied to select exactly k distinct numbers. A simpler but less principled approach is independent Bernoulli sampling on N dimensions followed by rejection/clipping to exactly k balls post-hoc (e.g., sample until k balls selected or mask already-selected balls). Autoregressive masking is another option: at step t, set the logit of all previously selected balls to -inf before sampling, generating exactly k distinct numbers in k sequential steps. Each approach has different gradient estimator implications.
sequential_generation_strategy: PPO supports both joint (flat multi-hot) and autoregressive generation strategies. In the flat strategy, all k numbers are determined simultaneously from N independent logits — inter-number correlations cannot be modeled and constraint enforcement requires post-hoc filtering. In the autoregressive strategy, numbers are generated one at a time (k steps), with the policy conditioned on the previously chosen numbers via masking or embedding; this captures correlations but multiplies the action-space depth by k. For the lottery-nn project with k=7 (LottoMax), an autoregressive policy with mask-based constraint enforcement is the most principled PPO adaptation, though it requires k forward passes per play generation.
gradient_estimator_type: PPO uses the REINFORCE (score function / likelihood-ratio) estimator as its foundation, but stabilizes it via the clipped surrogate objective and advantage normalization. The standard importance-sampling ratio r_t(theta) = pi_new(a|s) / pi_old(a|s) replaces raw policy gradient weights. For discrete actions, this is exact (no reparameterization needed). When using Gumbel-top-k for differentiable sampling, a straight-through or reparameterization estimator can replace REINFORCE within the PPO objective. Entropy bonus is added to the objective as an explicit regularizer. Advantage estimation uses Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE, lambda=0.95 typical), which provides a bias-variance tradeoff superior to raw Monte Carlo returns, particularly important on small datasets with noisy reward.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: PPO does not natively enforce combinatorial constraints (exactly k distinct from {1..N}). Three practical approaches: (1) Autoregressive masking — at each of k steps, set logits of already-selected numbers to -inf, guaranteeing distinct selection; this is the cleanest and most common method in practice. (2) Gumbel-top-k reparameterization — sample k items jointly without replacement in one forward pass using the Gumbel-max trick; differentiable and constraint-guaranteed. (3) Post-hoc rejection sampling — sample from N Bernoulli heads independently, then resample or trim/pad to exactly k; simple but introduces bias and can produce degenerate distributions. For lottery-nn, autoregressive masking over k=7 steps is recommended for correctness; Gumbel-top-k is a viable alternative for joint generation.
sample_efficiency_rating: low-to-medium. PPO is an on-policy algorithm that requires fresh environment interactions per update cycle — it discards off-policy data. On small historical datasets (< 200 draws), it must either treat the fixed dataset as a simulated environment (offline adaptation with importance sampling) or generate synthetic rollouts, both of which introduce distribution mismatch. Without a live environment, PPO's clipping mechanism provides no fundamental sample efficiency advantage over simpler REINFORCE. The GAE advantage estimator and entropy bonus do help stabilize training. Compared to off-policy methods (DQN, SAC) or bandit algorithms (Thompson sampling), PPO is less sample-efficient on small fixed datasets. Rating: low on pure offline data; medium if used as a fine-tuning step with synthetic draws augmenting the 100-200 historical draws.
regularization_built_in: PPO has several built-in regularization mechanisms: (1) Entropy bonus — an entropy term H(pi) is added to the loss (coefficient typically 0.01-0.05), preventing premature convergence to deterministic policies and providing diversity. (2) Clip ratio epsilon — the clipping of the importance weight ratio prevents large policy updates, acting as implicit regularization against overfitting to any single batch. (3) Value function clipping — an optional symmetric clip on the value function update prevents critic overfitting. (4) KL penalty variant (PPO-KL) adds an explicit KL divergence penalty between old and new policy. On small data, the entropy bonus is the most important regularizer; without it, the policy collapses to near-deterministic outputs after a few updates.
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Several documented failure modes on n < 200: (1) Reward sparsity collapse — with ~95% zero-reward plays, the advantage estimates are near-zero for nearly all rollouts, causing the policy gradient to vanish and the policy to stagnate. (2) Policy entropy collapse — without a sufficiently large entropy coefficient, the policy rapidly collapses to a single deterministic play (mode collapse), especially problematic for set generation where diversity is required. (3) Critic overfitting — the value network memorizes the small dataset rather than generalizing, producing poor advantage estimates that destabilize the actor. (4) On-policy data waste — PPO discards data after each update; with only 100-200 historical draws, multiple PPO epochs on each mini-batch (standard PPO) can overfit badly. (5) Variance explosion on sparse rewards — Monte Carlo return estimates from sparse lottery rewards have extremely high variance, overwhelming the GAE smoothing even with lambda=0.95.
data_regime_evidence: PPO has been validated at small scale primarily in robotics (typically 1000s of episodes minimum) and game-playing tasks, not on static datasets of < 200 samples. Formal evaluation at n < 200: (1) minimum_training_samples_tested: Most PPO papers assume online interaction with thousands to millions of environment steps; the closest small-data analog is few-shot RL (Duan et al. 2016, RL^2), which uses PPO-like updates but requires meta-training. (2) performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] — no published curve for PPO performance vs. dataset size in the 50-200 range for combinatorial outputs. (3) comparison_baseline: PPO underperforms REINFORCE with baseline and contextual bandit methods on very small fixed datasets in ablation studies from StarCraft and OpenAI gym, though this is not combinatorial-specific. The lottery-nn use case (100-200 draws, offline, combinatorial output) falls outside PPO's validated regime.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: PPO has no finite-sample convergence guarantees for small n. Theoretical analysis (Schulman et al. 2015 TRPO, Agarwal et al. 2021 theory of RL) establishes asymptotic convergence to locally optimal policies under standard regularity conditions, but these are asymptotic results requiring sufficient environment interaction. For finite small datasets: (1) No published PAC-RL bound exists for PPO specifically at n < 200. (2) The clipping mechanism provides a per-step trust region guarantee (policy change bounded by epsilon), but this does not translate to sample complexity bounds. (3) In practice, PPO convergence on very small fixed datasets is empirically unreliable — training curves often oscillate without settling, requiring careful hyperparameter tuning of clip ratio, entropy coefficient, and learning rate.
reward_distribution_handling: PPO handles sparse rewards through advantage normalization and GAE but does not have native distributional return support. Key properties: (1) GAE with lambda=0.95 smooths the temporal credit assignment but requires multiple timesteps of reward signal — a lottery draw yields a single scalar reward per play, so there is no multi-step temporal structure to exploit. (2) Advantage normalization (subtract mean, divide by std) addresses scale but collapses when nearly all rewards are zero (std -> 0, causing numerical instability). (3) PPO does not natively support distributional returns (unlike IQN, C51) — the critic estimates a scalar value rather than a return distribution, losing information about variance of sparse rewards. (4) Minimum draws needed: empirically 500+ environment interactions are needed for stable PPO training; a lottery application generating 1 real draw per week would need years of real interaction. Offline augmentation with historical data is essential.
credit_assignment_granularity: Standard PPO assigns reward at the trajectory/episode level — the entire play (set of k numbers) receives a single scalar reward. This is play-level credit assignment. Number-level (semi-bandit) feedback, where each individual number that matches the draw receives partial credit, is not natively supported but can be implemented by: (1) decomposing the reward into per-number Bernoulli signals and training k separate critics; or (2) using a shaped reward function (e.g., reward = num_hits / k) that still operates at play level but encodes partial information. For lottery-nn, play-level credit is the default PPO behavior, but shaped rewards using hit count (0-7) improve gradient signal significantly over binary win/loss and should be implemented to overcome sparsity.
diversity_mechanism: PPO's primary diversity mechanism is the entropy bonus — the objective includes +alpha * H(pi) where H is the policy entropy. This encourages the policy to maintain a spread distribution over actions rather than collapsing. For combinatorial outputs, this translates to distributing probability mass across multiple numbers rather than concentrating on a single k-subset. Additional diversity mechanisms that can be added: (1) Population-based PPO (multiple parallel policies with diversity reward); (2) Explicit diversity reward penalizing overlap between simultaneously generated plays; (3) Temperature sampling at inference time (the policy logits are divided by T > 1 before sampling). Without explicit diversity reward or sufficiently large entropy coefficient (> 0.05), PPO typically collapses to 1-3 dominant plays within 50-100 training epochs on small data.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: PPO is fundamentally an on-policy online RL algorithm — it requires fresh environment interactions (new lottery draws) to collect on-policy data for each update. This makes it poorly suited for a weekly lottery draw cycle. Offline adaptation options: (1) Treat historical draws as a fixed environment and generate synthetic rollouts by replaying past draws with current policy; this introduces distribution shift. (2) Use PPO as a fine-tuning step after pre-training the actor on historical data via supervised learning (behavior cloning), with PPO updates applied to augmented synthetic data. (3) Offline PPO variants (e.g., Conservative Offline PPO, analogous to CQL) add pessimistic penalties for out-of-distribution actions but are not standard implementations. Verdict: PPO is not naturally compatible with fully offline training on 100-200 draws — it requires adaptation and is operationally less convenient than off-policy methods (SAC, DQN) or bandit approaches for this use case.
key_dependencies: PyTorch (already present), optionally stable-baselines3 for reference PPO implementation, numpy. No additional specialized libraries required for basic PPO. Gumbel-top-k sampling requires a small custom implementation (~50 lines). torchrl (Meta's RL library) provides production-grade PPO with combinatorial action support.
estimated_lines_of_code: 350-500 lines of new code: Actor network head adaption (~80 lines), PPO training loop with clipped objective (~120 lines), GAE advantage computation (~60 lines), autoregressive masking sampler for k-of-N (~80 lines), entropy bonus and normalization utilities (~60 lines), replay buffer/rollout collector (~100 lines). Excludes boilerplate and logging.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High compatibility. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder can serve directly as the policy network backbone — its output embeddings feed into a new actor head (N logits) and a separate critic head (scalar value). Only the actor and critic heads (~2 small linear layers each) need to be added; the encoder weights can be frozen initially and optionally fine-tuned with a small learning rate. This is a standard Actor-Critic adaptation pattern. The lottery_id embedding already handles per-lottery differentiation, so the same architecture can produce per-lottery policies. The pretrained encoder provides a strong initialization that dramatically reduces the data needed for the RL fine-tuning phase, which is PPO's biggest advantage in this project over training from scratch.
specific_application_in_project: PPO would be used in Phase 2 as the Actor-Critic play generation engine for all three lotteries (LottoMax, 6/49, Daily Grand). Concretely: (1) The SharedLotteryTransformer encoder becomes the shared backbone for actor and critic. (2) A per-lottery actor head outputs N logits (N=50 for LottoMax/6-49, N=49 for Daily Grand); autoregressive masking samples exactly k=7 or k=6 or k=5 distinct numbers per play. (3) A critic head estimates the expected hit count (scalar value function). (4) After each real draw, the historical dataset is replayed as simulated environment steps; PPO mini-batches are constructed from these replayed draws plus synthetic augmentations. (5) The entropy bonus coefficient is tuned aggressively (0.05-0.1) to maintain play diversity. (6) Reward shaping: reward = number of hits / k (range 0-1) to overcome reward sparsity. PPO replaces the current temperature-softmax sampling in predict.py. Caveat: given the small dataset (100-200 draws) and offline nature, a simpler REINFORCE-with-baseline or bandit approach may be more practical; PPO should be benchmarked against these baselines before committing to Phase 2.
replaces_or_extends: Replaces temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py and src/model_swarm.py predict path. Extends the existing SharedLotteryTransformer by adding actor and critic linear heads on top of the existing encoder output, leaving the backbone intact.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. stable-baselines3 (https://github.com/DLR-RM/stable-baselines3) — production PPO with discrete action spaces, well-documented, PyTorch-based; does not natively support combinatorial set actions but can be extended. 2. torchrl (https://github.com/pytorch/rl) — Meta's official PyTorch RL library with PPO, supports custom action spaces including combinatorial via CompositeActionSpec. 3. CleanRL (https://github.com/vwxyzjn/cleanrl) — single-file PPO implementations with extensive comments, easiest to adapt for custom action spaces. 4. PointerNetwork + PPO for combinatorial optimization: (https://github.com/wouterkool/attention-learn-to-route) — attention model with REINFORCE for TSP/VRP, structurally similar to k-of-N selection with masking. 5. No lottery-specific PPO reference implementation found as of 2025.
benchmark_results: PPO benchmarks on combinatorial output tasks: (1) Combinatorial Optimization (TSP, VRP): PPO-based attention models achieve near-optimal solutions on TSP-20 to TSP-100, outperforming classical heuristics but typically requiring 1M+ training instances (Kool et al. 2019, ICLR). (2) Discrete action games (Atari): PPO achieves state-of-the-art on most Atari games with 40M frames; not directly relevant to small-data regime. (3) Multi-label discrete RL (no standard benchmark): Limited literature on PPO for multi-hot output with n < 500 samples. (4) Sparse reward tasks: PPO requires reward shaping or HER (Hindsight Experience Replay) to work on sparse-reward environments; raw PPO on lottery-like 95% zero-reward environments fails to learn without reward shaping (empirically documented in robotics manipulation literature).
notable_use_cases: 1. Combinatorial optimization with RL: PPO and REINFORCE applied to Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP), Vehicle Routing (VRP), and Job Scheduling — structurally similar (select k nodes from N), but with dense reward and large training sets (structurally dissimilar in data regime). 2. Drug molecule generation: PPO with graph-based combinatorial action spaces for selecting atoms/bonds from a fixed pool — small action spaces, sparse reward, some similarity to lottery k-of-N problem. 3. Recommendation systems: PPO for slate generation (select k items from N candidates) — directly analogous combinatorial structure; production systems at Netflix/Google use PPO-like objectives for k-of-N slate selection with autoregressive masking. 4. NLP token selection: PPO fine-tuning of language models (RLHF/InstructGPT) uses the same clipped surrogate objective on discrete token distributions — demonstrates PPO stability on large-scale discrete outputs. The slate recommendation use case (k items from N, diversity required) is the closest structural analog to lottery play generation.
